title: Ladder & Step-Ladder Safety
blurb: When a ladder is the right tool, how to check and set it up, and how to stay safe while on it.
siteNotes: Where ladders, step-ladders and any platforms or towers are kept
Who is trained or authorised to use them for each task
How to take a faulty ladder out of service and who to report it to
legalNotes: Work at height must be planned, use suitable equipment, and equipment must be inspected: Work at Height Regulations 2005. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/735
Staff duty to take reasonable care: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, s.7.

CHECK: the trainer says to have a colleague "foot" the ladder for higher or awkward tasks. HSE guidance prefers to secure (tie) a ladder, and footing is a fallback where tying is not possible; confirm the venue wording.

CHECK: the trainer says ladders suit "short, light jobs". HSE guidance describes ladders as low-risk, short-duration equipment, with a duration given in guidance; no figure is quoted here, so confirm what the venue wants stated.
CHECK: "surprising number of serious workplace falls" is the trainer's claim and no statistic is repeated.

cards.title: Ladder & Step-Ladder Safety
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- decide whether a ladder is the right tool
- check and set one up safely
- stay safe while you are on it

cards.title: Even a low fall can break bones
cards.body: Ladders and step-ladders are involved in a surprising number of serious workplace falls every year, and a fall from even a low height can break bones. It only takes a moment to set one up properly, and that is a lot quicker than recovering from a broken wrist.

cards.title: Ask first
cards.body: The first question is whether you need a ladder at all. For very quick, light jobs they are fine. For anything longer or higher, a proper platform or tower is safer.

right.title: Better to use a platform or tower for

cards.title: Check it first
cards.body: Look for damage before you use it. If it is faulty, do not use it. Take it out of service and report it.

items.title: Look it over
items.text: Bent stiles, cracked or missing feet, loose rungs.

items.title: Faulty?
items.text: Do not use it. Take it out of service.

items.title: Report it
items.text: So it is fixed or replaced.

cards.title: Firm, level and fully open
cards.body: Set it up on firm, level ground. With a step-ladder, make sure it is fully open and locked. Never use one half-folded or leaned against a wall.

cards.title: Three points of contact
cards.body: Keep three points of contact, which is two feet and a hand, or similar. Keep your body within the stiles (the side rails). Never stand on the very top step, and do not carry heavy or bulky items up.

items.title: Three points
items.text: Two feet and a hand, or similar.

items.title: No heavy loads
items.text: Do not carry bulky items up.

cards.title: Do not overreach
cards.body:
The classic mistake is overreaching. If you have to lean out to reach, get down and move the ladder. For anything higher or more awkward, have a colleague foot the ladder, and be aware of people and doors around you.

> If access looks unsafe, stop and report it rather than taking a chance.

items.title: Foot the ladder
items.text: A colleague steadies it for higher tasks.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Ask first: is a ladder the right tool?
- Check for damage, and report faulty ones
- Firm, level ground, step-ladder fully open and locked
- Three points of contact, within the stiles, never the top step
- Overreaching? Get down and move the ladder

cards.why: Ladders are fine for very quick, light jobs. Longer or higher jobs need a platform or tower.

cards.q: You should check a ladder for damage before using it.
cards.why: Look for bent stiles, cracked or missing feet and loose rungs before you climb.

cards.q: What does "three points of contact" mean?
options: Two feet and a hand on the ladder
Three rungs between you and the floor
Two hands and a foot on the wall
cards.why: Keep two feet and a hand, or similar, in contact with the ladder.

cards.q: It's okay to stand on the very top step of a step-ladder.
cards.why: Never stand on the very top step.

cards.q: If you can't quite reach something, you should…
options: Get down and move the ladder
Hold on with one hand and stretch
cards.why: Overreaching is the classic mistake. Get down and move the ladder instead.

cards.q: A step-ladder should be fully open and locked before use.
cards.why: Never use one half-folded or leaned against a wall.

cards.q: A ladder with a cracked foot should be…
options: Taken out of service and reported
Used only by the lightest person
cards.why: If a ladder is faulty, do not use it. Take it out of service and report it.

cards.q: Falls from height, even low ones, can cause serious injury.
cards.why: A fall from even a low height can break bones.

cards.q: What can a colleague do to help make a ladder more stable for a higher task?
options: Keep other staff talking to you
cards.why: For higher or more awkward tasks, have a colleague foot the ladder to steady it.

cards.q: Keeping your body within the stiles (side rails) helps prevent overbalancing.
cards.why: Staying within the stiles keeps your weight over the ladder.
